newsitem.title: UK: Cocoa price to rise as stock/consumption falls - EIU.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa price to rise as stock/consumption falls - EIU.

text.p: Cocoa prices should rise in years ahead as the stock to consumption ratio falls to its lowest level since 1985/86, said the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU).

"We are now forecasting bigger deficits in 1996/97, 1997/98 and 1998/99, which means that the ratio of stocks to consumption will fall to its lowest since 35.6 percent in 1985/86," it said in its second-quarter report on world commodity markets.

But the group noted that stocks would still likely remain above the key 30-percent level and that price rises should start from a lower-than-expected base due to West African producers' selling to take advantage of sterling's strength.

Nevertheless, it said prices have "become more bullish, considering that annual sales from the ICCO's (International Cocoa Organization) stockpile will end in March 1998 and that an estimated 300,000 tons of commercial cocoa stock is controlled by just one trading house."
Though it predicts world production to inch up in 1997/98, it said the general underproduction plaguing the 1990s should continue through the end of the decade and weigh on stocks.
For 1996/97, available data for the Ivory Coast's main crop and generally good weather for the mid-crop pointed to production of at least one million tons, the group said.
Good soil moisture in Cameroon and Nigeria for the second consecutive year is expected to continue boosting production there from first-half 1990s levels.
But dry weather has harmed prospects in Ghana, where no more than 330,000 tons is expected.
In Brazil, EIU revised down its overall forecast to 190,000 tons because of a poor mid-crop outlook and expectations for a considerable drop in the main crop from 1995/96.
E D & F Man estimates Brazil's 1996/97 output at 156,000 tons, a 20-year low. The ICCO predicts 195,000 tons.

In Asia, Malaysia is seen recovering and Indonesia posting a record harvest. The ICCO predicts Malaysia to produce 120,000 tons and Indonesia to bring in 330,000 tons. E D & F Man expects 110,000 tons and 310,000 tons, respectively.

On the demand side, EIU raised its forecast for 1996/97 consumption to 2.79 million tons to account for upward revisions in recent estimated use, an upward grinding trend and lower-than-expected prices. That compares with ICCO's 2.82 million-ton forecast and E D & F Man's 2.76-million ton prediction.
But EIU noted that as cocoa prices rise, consumption should grow more slowly in 1997/98 and decline in 1998/99.

So far this year, EIU said chocolate manufacturers have been light buyers because they are drawing on stocks built in 1995/96. It said the drop in fourth-quarter western European grindings reflected this, not slowing final consumption.

EIU said forecasts reflect higher production bases in the Ivory Coast and Ghana in the past few years from replanting, high-yielding hybrids and market reforms, continued Indonesian expansion and some recovery in Brazil as the government spends more on fighting witches' broom disease.
